title: Letter 27 — Guard Against Despair
attribution_note: Letter 27 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

sections.heading: The bitter fruits of sin, and the mercy of God

pairs.en: I hear that thoughts trouble your conscience and draw you toward despair. Behold the fruits of sins! It is sweet to a man to sin, but bitter to taste the fruits of sins.

Beware of despairing! Despair is a heavy sin, and a sin against the mercy of God. God the Lover of mankind *“will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.”* [1 Timothy 2:4] Why, then, despair? God calls all to repentance, and to those who repent He promises and wills to show mercy. [see Matthew 4:17; 11:28] And if the sinner turns from his sins, and repents of them and grieves for them, and guards himself against further sins — this is what God wills, and this is pleasing to Him; and upon such a sinner God looks mercifully, and forgives him all his sins, and remembers them no more.

Thus God Himself bears witness of this in Holy Scripture, saying: *“But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed... he shall surely live, he shall not die.* *All his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him.”* [Ezekiel 18:21–22] What is more comforting than this to repenting sinners? All their sins and iniquities are already remembered no more before God. Glory to the loving-kindness of God, that He remembers not our sins and iniquities when we turn from them and repent! And since the sins and iniquities of the repenting are not remembered, the former lawless life harms them no longer. For they are as those who have come up out of a pit and walk upon level ground, or as those who have come out of darkness into the light, or as those who have been set free from captivity and from prison and have received their liberty. For the sinner, while he works lawlessness, walks in darkness and is as in a pit of perdition; but if he begins to repent of his sins and to guard himself against every sin, he is delivered from all that misery.
And that thoughts trouble you — this is profitable for you.
1) Such thoughts humble and bruise your heart, which is needful for repentance.

2) They hold you back from sins, both those that were before and those that remain. How will you sin, tasting such bitter fruits of sin? Who does not beware of a serpent, knowing the venom of its sting? Who touches the fire, knowing that it burns and scorches? How, then, shall a man sin, feeling that sin is so bitter?
3) Such thoughts turn a man away from the world, from its vanity and its deceit.
4) They move him to heartfelt and earnest prayer, which a Christian needs, and so forth.

sections.heading: Keep the path you have begun

pairs.en: Repent, then, and strive against despair, and wait upon the mercy of God — only beware with all care that you return not to what was before. Satan will draw you with all his strength back to your former lawless life; but stand firm in what you have begun, take courage and be strong, and pray earnestly concerning this. Read often, with attention and zeal: *“Have mercy upon me, O God,”* and the rest [Psalm 50], and the other psalm: *“Make haste, O God, to help me,”* and the rest [Psalm 69]. Shun evil companies and friendships. Go not into a monastery. Let your house and solitude be to you in place of a monastery. Withdraw often from those of your household, and in solitude bend the knee before God, and fall down before Him in humility, and pray to Him with the publican's voice: *“God be merciful to me a sinner!”* [Luke 18:13]

And again I repeat: beware of bitter despair, and beware of returning to your former life; but go by that path which you have begun, and you will come to a blessed end and to eternal life — which I earnestly desire for you. Remember me also, a sinner, in your kneelings. The Lord help you in all things. Commending myself and you to Him, I remain
Your well-wisher, Tikhon, unworthy bishop.
